title: Healing ceremony unites Abbotsford Police with family of woman who died in custody
article: Abbotsford Police Deputy Chief Rick Lucy stood at a coroner's inquest last month and apologized to the family of Christine Bernadette Miller, 39, who died in August 2008 while in police custody.
Lucy said Miller had come into their care to keep her safe.
"We failed in our effort to do that," he said to the 25 or so family members attending the inquest from Oct. 26 to 28 in Burnaby.
That admission and apology opened the way for an event that was a first for the Abbotsford Police Department (APD) - and perhaps across the nation.

On Nov. 13, a traditional First Nations "healing ceremony" was held between about 10 APD members and 40 members of Miller's family. Much of it took place in the APD detention cell where Miller, who belonged to the Skwah First Nation in Chilliwack, was detained after being arrested for public intoxication.
She was found in medical distress and taken to hospital, but died. Her death was the result of a toxic mix of codeine, acetaminophen, ethanol, diphenhydramine and diazepam, the coroner determined.

The healing ceremony was conducted by Chief Willie Charlie of the Chehalis Indian Band. The sacred ritual included drumming, singing and praying. He said one of the purposes was to release Miller to the "spirit world."
"It's to gather up any part of her spirit that might be left and make herself whole for her journey to the other side," he said.

Charlie said another purpose was to provide a sense of closure for the family, so they can move on with their healing. Part of that process included being able to forgive the people they deemed responsible for her death.

Lucy said the APD officers involved in the case carried a heavy burden over Miller's death. When the APD was told the family wanted to hold a healing ceremony and include police, they didn't hesitate.
"It was the right thing to do," Lucy said.

Also participating were Police Chief Bob Rich, Deputy Chief Len Goerke and Mayor George Peary, who chairs the police board. Chief Alice McKay from Matsqui First Nation and Chief Dalton Silver from Sumas First Nation also attended.

Charlie said there was a "lot of heaviness" and tension at the start of the proceedings. Lucy said although police were "very honoured and genuinely moved" to be involved, there was some apprehension about what would happen.
Those feelings eased as the ceremony progressed, and the songs and drumming echoed through the empty jail cell. It was powerful to feel the family's forgiveness, Lucy said. Peary agreed.
"I think it was historic. It was momentous," he said of the ceremony.
Charlie said the event was particularly significant considering the tattered relationship between police and First Nations people over the years.

"The tensions are very, very high, and there's been a lot of mistrust. This ceremony went a very, very long way (to repairing that)," he said, adding that he hopes it serves as a "template" for other police departments and First Nations bands.
The event concluded with a lunch at Clearbrook Library. By that time, the unity of the two sides was clearly evident, Charlie said.
"I think the feelings at the end were that there was a real coming together, a real good feeling, a lot more respect for one another."
